Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette: Mr. Thompson is a 66-year-old married European-American man who works as a software engineer and has been experiencing significant distress following childhood physical abuse by his caregiver. His current state reflects a deeply entrenched set of symptoms that have significantly impacted his daily life. The traumatic event occurred during his childhood when he was frequently subjected to violent outbursts from an abusive caregiver. The specific triggers associated with this trauma are vivid and intensely disturbing: the sensation of a sudden change in skin temperature, the rapid pounding of his own heart, and intrusive memories of the event surfacing unbidden. These triggers often transport him back to those terrifying moments, making it difficult for him to differentiate between past and present. For instance, when Mr. Thompson feels a sudden chill on his skin or notices his heart racing, he is instantly transported back to the times when his caregiver would suddenly lash out, causing his body to react before his mind could fully process what was happening. The unexpected touch from someone now triggers a startle response that is immediate and intense, making him feel as though he must be hyper-vigilant at all times. Mr. Thompson’s hyper-vigilance has led him to avoid situations where these triggers might be activated. He avoids social interactions, especially with people he once knew before the traumatic event, because seeing them reminds him of his isolation and makes him question whether anyone can truly be trusted. Additionally, he tries to stay away from any form of physical contact, even friendly touches, as they bring back memories of the abuse and make him feel unsafe. The sense of being an outsider permeates his life, making it difficult for him to trust others or engage in social activities. He believes that everyone around him could potentially turn hostile at any moment, which has led him to adopt strategies such as avoiding physical contact and staying away from people he knows. This avoidance has resulted in a gradual withdrawal from social circles and even from his own body, as he avoids paying attention to it due to the fear of being reminded of the abuse. His constant state of vigilance also manifests in his heightened awareness of potential dangers. He is always on guard for weapons or any objects that could be used as threats, which further reinforces his negative appraisals and leads him to believe that danger lurks around every corner. This belief in turn fuels his maladaptive strategies, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where he is constantly on edge. Over time, these strategies have taken a toll on Mr. Thompson’s life, particularly at work. As a software engineer, the constant need for vigilance and avoidance has made it difficult to focus on tasks that require collaboration with others or involve physical interaction with equipment. He finds himself increasingly isolated in his role, which exacerbates his sense of being an outsider. Mr. Thompson finally sought help because he realized that his symptoms were becoming more severe and interfering significantly with his daily life. What frightens him most is the prospect of never feeling safe again, but what gives him hope is the possibility of finding a way to break free from this cycle of fear and isolation. He hopes that through therapy, he can learn how to manage his triggers, reduce his vigilance, and ultimately reconnect with others in a meaningful way. The narrative of Mr. Thompson's journey highlights the intricate interplay between his triggers, maladaptive strategies, negative appraisals, and heightened threat perception. Each element feeds into the other, creating a complex web that has ensnared him over time. The goal now is to help him unravel these connections and find a path towards healing and safety.
